opus-5.5.text:
I think Operator is an intermediate form because it's essentially asking an AI to use a computer the way a human does: look at the screen, move the mouse, click buttons, type into forms. That's a very natural starting point, because the whole digital world today is built for human eyes and human hands. If you want an agent to be useful right now, without waiting for every website to expose a clean interface, then operating the GUI directly is the most general approach. So it makes a lot of sense as a first step.

But if you think about it from first principles, it's not the most efficient way for an agent to work. A screen is a visual representation designed for humans. For a model, parsing pixels, locating a button, and clicking it is a pretty roundabout way to accomplish what could be a single API call or a few lines of code. It's slow, it's brittle — a layout change or a pop-up can break the whole flow — and it consumes a lot of compute for something conceptually simple. It's a bit like the early days of cars being designed to look like horse carriages. You're mapping the new technology onto the old interface.

There's also the human interaction side. Right now with Operator, you give it a task and then you kind of sit there watching it click around, and occasionally it stops and asks you to take over, for example to log in or confirm a payment. That interaction pattern is awkward. You're neither fully delegating nor doing it yourself. In the long run, I think the ideal is that you express your intent, the agent goes off and does things asynchronously — possibly many things in parallel — and only comes back to you when it genuinely needs a decision or when the result is ready.

So my view is that the end state will look different on both ends. On the environment side, more and more services will become agent-native: APIs, protocols, structured interfaces designed for models rather than for people. On the interaction side, the agent becomes more like a capable colleague or assistant you delegate to, rather than a remote-controlled cursor you watch. GUI operation will still matter as a fallback for the long tail of things that don't have a better interface, but it won't be the main way agents get work done.

Operator is valuable because it shows the capability is real — models can actually perceive and act in complex environments, and that's exactly what reinforcement learning helps with. But it's a transitional product, a bridge between the world built for humans and a world where agents are first-class participants.

r001.rationale: The response describes future agent-native APIs and protocols, but does not propose using Operator to establish an entry point that an agent can later call directly.

r002.rationale: It says GUI operation is roundabout for agents, slow, brittle, and compute-intensive compared with API calls or code.

r003.rationale: It explains that GUI operation is broadly useful now because the digital world is built for human eyes and hands, and many services lack clean interfaces.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, Operator is a very natural thing for OpenAI to ship at this moment, and I think it's valuable, but I'd call it a transitional product rather than the final shape of how people will interact with agents.

Look at what it actually does. It opens a browser, it looks at the screen, it clicks buttons, it fills in forms, essentially the way a human would. The reason it works that way is not because that's the ideal interface for a model. It's because the entire internet was built for humans with eyes and a mouse. The model is being forced to adapt to an environment designed for us. That's an enormous amount of wasted effort. You're spending huge compute to parse pixels and figure out where the "checkout" button is, when the underlying task is just "buy this item for this price." Any time a system has to pretend to be a human to get things done, that tells you the infrastructure hasn't caught up yet.

So why do it at all? Because it's the fastest way to get coverage. You can't wait for every website and every service in the world to expose a clean API to agents. Browser control gives you a universal, if clumsy, adapter. It's a bit like the early days of RPA, robotic process automation, where companies wrote scripts to click through legacy software. That was never elegant, but it bridged the gap until systems got proper integrations.

What I expect to happen is that the world gradually reorganizes itself around agents. Services will start exposing structured interfaces designed for models, not for people. You already see early signs of this with things like tool-calling protocols and companies thinking about an "agent-facing" version of their product. Once that happens, an agent won't need to look at a screen and move a cursor. It'll just call the function directly. Faster, cheaper, far more reliable.

There's also a second dimension, which is the interaction between the agent and the user. Right now with Operator you're kind of watching over its shoulder, and you intervene when it gets stuck or hits a login page. That supervision model is also intermediate. It reflects the fact that we don't fully trust the agent yet, and the agent doesn't yet know when it should ask versus when it should proceed. As models get better at long-horizon reasoning and at understanding their own uncertainty, that relationship shifts. You give an intention, and you come back to a result.

So I'd summarize it this way: Operator is what you build when the models are already fairly capable but the world around them is not yet ready. It demonstrates the demand and it collects a lot of real interaction data, which is valuable in itself. But the long-term form will look much less like a robot using a human's computer, and much more like software talking to software, with the human only stating what they want.

r001.rationale: The response says Operator provides broad browser coverage and predicts agents will later call structured functions directly, but it does not propose using Operator to establish an entry point that agents can subsequently call.

r002.rationale: It describes screen parsing and locating buttons as “a huge amount of wasted effort” and says browser control is clumsy compared with direct function calls.

r003.rationale: It explains that Operator uses a browser because the internet was built for humans with eyes and a mouse, and that browser control offers coverage while services lack agent APIs.

astra-6.text:
I see Operator as an intermediate form because it acts through an interface designed for humans. It looks at the screen, clicks buttons, and types into fields. That’s a useful way to make an agent work with existing websites without requiring every service to build a new integration.

But the graphical interface adds an extra layer. If I ask an agent to book a trip, the underlying task is to find options, compare constraints, and make a reservation. Clicking through pages is just how a human currently accesses those capabilities. An agent could eventually do much of that through structured interfaces, with clearer information about what actions are available and whether they succeeded.

So Operator is a bridge: it lets agents operate in today’s digital environment. Over time, I expect more services to expose capabilities directly to agents, while people remain involved in setting goals and approving consequential decisions. Visual interaction will still be useful, especially for older systems, but it probably won’t be the only—or always the primary—way agents get things done.

r001.rationale: The response says Operator bridges agents to existing websites and anticipates direct structured interfaces, but does not propose using Operator to establish an entry point the agent can later call directly.

r002.rationale: It describes the graphical interface as an extra layer over the underlying task and says agents could use clearer structured interfaces, communicating that GUI interaction is less direct and efficient for agents.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says Operator uses an interface designed for humans and lets agents work with today’s websites, which explains its broad applicability.

sol-6.1.text:
I see Operator as an intermediate form because it lets an AI act through interfaces that were designed for humans. It looks at a screen, clicks buttons, and types into forms. That’s useful because it can work with existing websites without requiring every service to build a new integration.

But I don’t think clicking through a graphical interface is necessarily the final form of agent interaction. If an agent wants to book a flight, what matters is communicating the destination, constraints, and authorization, then getting a reliable result. It shouldn’t always need to reproduce every step a person would take on a website.

Over time, I expect more services to expose interfaces designed for agents, with clearer ways to express intent, grant permissions, and verify outcomes. So Operator is a bridge: it gives agents access to today’s digital world while that world gradually adapts to agents.

r001.rationale: The response calls Operator a bridge to future agent-designed interfaces, but does not say it establishes an entry point the agent can later call directly.

r002.rationale: It says an agent should not always have to reproduce every step a person takes on a website, communicating that graphical interaction is less efficient for agents.

r003.rationale: It explains that Operator works with existing websites because they were designed for human users, so it applies without requiring services to build new integrations.
